notes.summary: Chemistry gives about 1 to 2 questions per paper. Past papers ask most about acids, bases and reactions, atoms and the periodic table, metals and everyday chemistry, and carbon compounds. The highest-scoring lists are common names and formulas, natural acids, ores and alloys: learn them as tables.

concepts.title: Matter and separation
concepts.body:
• States: solid, liquid, gas, plasma and Bose-Einstein condensate (predicted by S.N. Bose and Albert Einstein, 1924 to 1925).
  • Sublimation (solid straight to gas): camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice.
  • Element (one kind of atom), compound (fixed ratio, new properties), mixture (any ratio, can be separated).
  • True solution (salt in water), colloid (milk, fog, smoke, butter; shows the Tyndall effect), suspension (muddy water; particles settle).
Separation methodUsed for
DistillationPure water from salt water
Fractional distillationPetroleum into fractions; gases from liquid air
ChromatographyColours in ink or dyes
CentrifugationCream from milk; blood tests
CrystallisationPure salt or copper sulphate
SublimationCamphor or ammonium chloride from salt
Separating funnelOil from water

concepts.title: Atomic structure
concepts.body:
• Dalton's atomic theory (1808). Thomson's 'plum pudding' model. Rutherford's nuclear model (1911). Bohr's model with fixed energy shells.
  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons (idea of Moseley). Mass number = protons + neutrons.
  • Shell capacity is 2n²: K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 18.
  • Isotopes: same atomic number, different mass number (protium, deuterium, tritium; carbon-12 and carbon-14). Isobars: same mass number, different atomic number (argon-40 and calcium-40).
  • An ion with positive charge is a cation; with negative charge, an anion (for example Cl−, with charge −1).
  • Avogadro's number: 6.022 × 1023 particles in one mole.
  • Charles's law (about 1787): volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature at fixed pressure. Boyle's law: P × V is constant at fixed temperature.

concepts.title: Periodic table
concepts.body:
• Dobereiner's triads, Newlands' law of octaves, then Mendeleev (1869) arranged elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements (eka-aluminium became gallium, eka-silicon became germanium). He could not give hydrogen or isotopes a correct place.
  • Modern periodic law (Moseley): properties depend on atomic number. 18 groups and 7 periods; 118 elements.
  • Group 1: alkali metals. Group 2: alkaline earth metals. Group 17: halogens. Group 18: noble gases. Lanthanides (atomic numbers 57 to 71, for example cerium, neodymium) and actinides (89 to 103, for example thorium, uranium, plutonium) sit below the table.
  • Across a period (left to right): atomic size falls, metallic character falls. Down a group: size rises, metallic character rises. Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
  • Element 106, seaborgium, is named after Glenn T. Seaborg.
RecordElement
Lightest; most abundant in the universeHydrogen
Most abundant in Earth's crustOxygen, then silicon, then aluminium (most abundant metal), then iron
Most abundant in airNitrogen
Liquid metal; liquid non-metal at room temperatureMercury; bromine
Best conductor of electricitySilver
Lightest metal; densest metalLithium; osmium
Highest melting point metalTungsten
Hardest natural substanceDiamond (carbon)
Non-metal that conducts electricityGraphite (carbon)

Latin symbols: Na natrium (sodium), K kalium (potassium), Fe ferrum (iron), Cu cuprum (copper), Ag argentum (silver), Au aurum (gold), Pb plumbum (lead), Sn stannum (tin), Hg hydrargyrum (mercury), W wolfram (tungsten).

concepts.title: Bonding and chemical reactions
concepts.body:
• Ionic bond: transfer of electrons (NaCl). Covalent bond: sharing of electrons (H2O, CH4, Cl2).
Reaction typeExample
CombinationQuicklime + water → slaked lime (also exothermic)
Decomposition (heat)CaCO3 → CaO + CO2
Decomposition (light)Silver chloride turns grey in sunlight (used in black-and-white photography)
Decomposition (electricity)Electrolysis of water
DisplacementIron nail in copper sulphate turns brown; solution turns green
Double displacement (precipitation)BaCl2 + Na2SO4 gives white barium sulphate
RedoxOxidation: gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction: the opposite
Exothermic / endothermicBurning and respiration give out heat; photosynthesis takes it in
  • Corrosion: rusting of iron needs both air and water; rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Rancidity: oxidation of fats; chip packets are filled with nitrogen to prevent it.
  • Catalysts: nickel in hydrogenation of vegetable oils (vanaspati ghee); iron in the Haber process (ammonia); vanadium pentoxide in the contact process (sulphuric acid). Enzymes are biological catalysts.
  • Water treatment: alum is added for flocculation (settling of particles); chlorine or bleaching powder kills germs.

concepts.title: Acids, bases and pH
concepts.body:
• Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red. Bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue. Water-soluble bases are alkalis.
  • Indicators: phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base; turmeric turns reddish-brown in base.
  • pH scale (S.P.L. Sørensen): 0 to 14. Below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. Each step is a tenfold change.
  • Approximate pH: stomach acid 1 to 2, lemon juice about 2, vinegar about 3, pure water 7, human blood 7.35 to 7.45, sea water about 8, milk of magnesia about 10, sodium hydroxide about 14.
  • Tooth enamel starts to decay when mouth pH falls below about 5.5. Antacids (milk of magnesia) neutralise extra stomach acid.
  • Aqua regia (3 parts HCl : 1 part HNO3) dissolves gold and platinum. Sulphuric acid is called the 'king of chemicals'.
AcidNatural source

concepts.title: Metals and non-metals
concepts.body:
• Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors. Exceptions: mercury is liquid; sodium and potassium are soft and are stored in kerosene; gold is the most malleable and ductile.
  • Non-metals are mostly brittle and poor conductors. Exceptions: graphite conducts; iodine is lustrous; diamond is the hardest. White phosphorus is stored in water.
  • Reactivity series (most to least): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Au. A metal displaces any metal below it from its salt solution.
  • Extraction: froth flotation concentrates sulphide ores; roasting (heating sulphide ores in air) and calcination (heating carbonate ores in limited air); reduction by carbon or electrolysis; refining by electrolysis.
  • Corrosion protection: galvanisation (zinc coat on iron), tinning, painting, oiling, electroplating, anodising (oxide layer on aluminium). Silver tarnishes black (silver sulphide); copper gets a green coat (basic copper carbonate).

concepts.title: Carbon compounds
concepts.body:
• Allotropes of carbon: diamond (hardest, does not conduct), graphite (soft, conducts, used as lubricant and pencil 'lead'), fullerene C60 (buckminsterfullerene), graphene. Carbon forms long chains (catenation).
  • Hydrocarbons: alkanes have single bonds (methane, ethane, propane, butane); alkenes have a double bond (ethene, used to ripen fruit); alkynes have a triple bond (ethyne or acetylene, used in welding).
  • Functional groups: −OH alcohol; −CHO aldehyde; C=O ketone; −COOH carboxylic acid; −Cl, −Br halo group.
  • Ethanol is drinking alcohol; mixing in methanol (which can cause blindness) makes it unfit to drink (denatured spirit). Ethanoic acid (acetic acid) is in vinegar (about 5 to 8%). Acid + alcohol gives sweet-smelling esters.
  • Friedrich Wöhler made urea from an inorganic compound (1828), the first organic synthesis. Hermann Kolbe synthesised acetic acid (1845).
  • Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of fatty acids, made by saponification. They form scum in hard water; detergents work in hard water.
  • Hard water: temporary hardness (bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium) is removed by boiling; permanent hardness (chlorides and sulphates) by washing soda or ion exchange.

concepts.title: Fuels and polymers
concepts.body:
• CNG is mainly methane. LPG is mainly butane and propane; ethyl mercaptan is added so leaks can be smelt. Biogas (gobar gas) is mainly methane.
  • Coal ranks by carbon content: peat, lignite, bituminous, anthracite (best). Coal gives coke, coal tar and coal gas.
  • Petroleum is refined by fractional distillation into LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, paraffin wax and bitumen.
  • Hydrogen has the highest calorific value. Octane number rates petrol (resistance to knocking); cetane number rates diesel.
  • Producer gas = CO + N2. Water gas = CO + H2.
PolymerFact
Natural rubberPolymer of isoprene; vulcanised with sulphur (Charles Goodyear) to make it hard
NylonFirst fully synthetic fibre
Polyester (terylene)Clothes, PET bottles
RayonArtificial silk made from cellulose (wood pulp)

Thermoplastics soften on heating (polythene, PVC); thermosetting plastics do not (Bakelite, melamine).

concepts.body:
GasFact

Carbon dioxideFire extinguishers, soft drinks, dry ice
Hydrogen sulphideRotten egg smell
Methyl isocyanateBhopal gas tragedy (1984)
Helium; neon; argonBalloons; advertising signs; filled in bulbs
AmmoniaFertilisers (Haber process)
ChlorineBleaching, disinfecting water
  • Fertilisers: urea (about 46% nitrogen, the highest), DAP, ammonium sulphate, NPK.
  • Glass: silica + sodium carbonate + limestone. Colours: cobalt oxide (blue), chromium oxide (green). Borosilicate (Pyrex) resists heat. Cement: Portland cement by Joseph Aspdin; gypsum is added to slow setting.
  • Food: baking powder = baking soda + tartaric acid; preservatives: salt, sugar, vinegar, sodium benzoate; sweeteners: saccharin, aspartame, sucralose; iodised salt contains potassium iodate.
  • Medicines: analgesics relieve pain (aspirin, paracetamol); antipyretics lower fever; antibiotics kill bacteria (penicillin, Alexander Fleming, 1928); antacids neutralise acid; antiseptics on skin (Dettol, tincture of iodine, boric acid); disinfectants on objects (phenol). Agonists mimic the body's messenger at a receptor; antagonists block the receptor.
  • Silver iodide is used for cloud seeding. Acid rain (from SO2 and nitrogen oxides) damages marble, as at the Taj Mahal.

varieties.name: Matter, atoms and the periodic table
varieties.how: Know what changes across a period and down a group, the group names, and the record elements. For atoms, use protons for atomic number and protons plus neutrons for mass number.

example.q: Atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called:
steps: Same atomic number means the same element.
Different mass numbers mean different neutrons: isotopes.

varieties.name: Reactions, acids, bases and pH
varieties.how: Place the substance on the pH scale (below 7 acid, above 7 base). For natural acids, link the food to the acid. For reactions, name the type from what happens to the reactants.

example.q: Which acid is present in an ant sting?
steps: Ant and nettle stings inject a simple acid.
It is formic acid, also called methanoic acid.

varieties.name: Metals, ores and alloys
varieties.how: Learn alloy and its metals, ore and its metal. Note that German silver has no silver and cinnabar is mercury.

varieties.name: Common names and formulas
varieties.how: Learn the common name, chemical name and formula together. Group by metal: sodium (salt, baking soda, washing soda), calcium (lime family, gypsum, POP), sulphates (the vitriols).

steps: Heating gypsum to about 100 °C gives the hemihydrate CaSO4·½H2O.

varieties.name: Carbon compounds, fuels and polymers
varieties.how: Know functional groups by their symbols, the main gas in each fuel, and one use of each polymer.

example.q: Which class of compounds has the functional group −OH?
steps: −COOH is a carboxylic acid; −CHO is an aldehyde.

varieties.name: Chemistry in everyday life
varieties.how: Link each household use to its chemical (what kills germs, what makes cakes rise, what gives a smell). For spices, learn the active compound list.

example.q: Eugenol is the main compound in which spice?
steps: Curcumin is turmeric; piperine is black pepper.

tips: Reactivity series: 'Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra, I Like Her Calling Me A Smart Goat' (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au).
Vitriols by colour: blue copper, green iron, white zinc.
Bronze is the older alloy (Bronze Age) and uses tin; brass uses zinc.
Crust order: 'O Si Al Fe' (oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron).
Indicators: phenolphthalein turns pink in base; methyl orange turns red in acid.
Isotopes keep the atomic number (same 'P'), isobars keep the mass number (same 'bar' weight).
traps: Baking soda is NaHCO3; washing soda is Na2CO3·10H2O.
Cinnabar is the ore of mercury, not copper; galena is lead.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide, not frozen water.
Roasting heats sulphide ores in plenty of air; calcination heats carbonate ores in limited air.

questions.q: The chemical name of common salt is:
questions.solution:
Common salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.
Memory hook: Na + Cl = the salt on your table.

questions.q: The pH of pure water at 25 °C is:
questions.solution:
Pure water is neutral, pH 7. Below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic.
Memory hook: 7 sits in the middle of 0–14.

questions.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.solution:
Mercury (Hg) is the only metal liquid at room temperature. Bromine is the liquid non-metal.
Memory hook: Mercury's old name is 'quicksilver' — silver that flows.

questions.q: Which acid is found in an ant sting?
questions.solution:
Ant and nettle stings contain methanoic acid (formic acid). A mild base like baking soda gives relief.
Memory hook: Formica is Latin for ant — formic acid.

Brass = copper + zinc. Bronze = copper + tin. Solder = lead + tin.
Memory hook: Brass taps shine with zinc; the bronze medal is cast with tin.

questions.q: Which compound is known as 'laughing gas'?
questions.solution:
Nitrous oxide (N2O) is laughing gas, used as a mild anaesthetic.
Memory hook: N2O — 'two N's make you grin'.

Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO4·½H2O. Heating gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) gives it; adding water sets it back into gypsum.
Memory hook: 'Hemi' = half a water.

Cinnabar (HgS) is the ore of mercury, not copper.
Memory hook: Cinnabar is the bright red ore from which quicksilver (mercury) is roasted out.
